title: Farid close
hookLine: a Sufi's humility near the end of the Guru's book: become the grass on the path

lines: A SUFI NEAR THE END OF THE BOOK.
cards: Turn toward the last pages of the Guru Granth Sahib, among the short couplets, and a Muslim saint of the Punjab is still speaking there, signing his lines with his own name: Farid.
This path has sat with him through a tree on a riverbank, a heart like a jewel, dry bread and cool water, a collar to look under before judging anyone.
Today we close his pages with the thing under all the others: how low a person is willing to go.

teach.h: BECOME THE GRASS ON THE PATH.
teach.b: One of Farid's couplets, from Ang 1378, in paraphrase: Farid, if you long for the Lord of all, become the grass on the path. One person cuts it, another tramples it. Then you'll be let into the Master's court.
Grass by a footpath doesn't argue, or keep a list of who walked on it.
It gets cut and grows back, low enough that nobody notices it, steady enough that the path stays green. Farid asks to be that. Now a careful second turn.
Some readers worry this sounds like letting people walk all over you. But look at the Farid of these days.
The same man told us to look under our own collar, and said that those with one thing in the heart and another on the lips are false. That isn't a doormat talking. His humility is sharp.

It's the self that insists on being seen that he wants to lower, not the truth he's willing to say. The third turn is where these lines live: a Sufi of the Punjab, inside the book Sikhs bow to as their living Guru.
Sikhs have a word for the quality Farid keeps returning to: nimrata, humility.
Tradition says the Gurus treasured his verses, and the book keeps them near its close, in his own Punjabi, with his name in the lines.
So his pages end not with a crown, but with grass, and a path, and a door that opens for the one who's willing to be low.

how: Farid's couplets are read and sung in gurdwaras as gurbani alongside the Gurus' own hymns, and Sikhs often draw on them when speaking about nimrata, humility.

o: silence: never saying a hard truth to anyone at all
obedience to whoever happens to have power over you
humility, like grass on a path that's cut and grows back

games.q: a week with Farid — tap the pairs.
p: a jewel not to be broken

s: Farid's couplets sit in the Guru Granth Sahib with his own name on them
he signs his lines Farid, in his own Punjabi.
the grass couplet means never saying anything hard to anyone
the same Farid tells us to look under our own collar and calls the double-hearted false. his humility is sharp.

games.q: Farid wants to reach the Lord of all. which picture does he choose for himself?
o: a tall tree that everyone can see.
the grass on the path, cut and trampled.
a lamp set high on a wall.
games.why: become the grass on the path, he says. one cuts it, another tramples it, and then it's let into the Master's court.

practice: Choose one of Farid's lines from these days, the tree on the riverbank, every heart a jewel, dry bread and cool water, the collar, or the grass on the path, and say it slowly, once.

Then sit with it, letting your breath go out longer than it comes in, the way grass bends; if one line keeps tugging at you, that's the one to keep. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Nimrata. Humility, the quality Farid's couplets keep returning to: not a crown, but grass that lets itself be cut and trampled, steady enough to keep the path green.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: nimrata, humility, the quality Farid's couplets keep returning to.

carryVoice: Your line: humble to the end. Low like grass, and still green. Farid's pages, closed.
